title: Architecture: Effect of Territory, Boundary, and Orientation on Family Functioning.
authors: Suzanne H. Crowhurst Lennard et al., 1977
central_proposition: The physical home environment significantly influences and is influenced by family interaction, role relationships, values, and identities, operating through concepts of territory, boundary, and orientation, which can exhibit isomorphic, complementary, or non-fitting relationships with family dynamics.

concept_definitions.name: Isomorphic Fit
concept_definitions.definition: A relationship where both family interaction and environment exhibit similarities in shape, pattern, or form, achieving similar effects, and where environmental aspects are clear expressions of the family's identity, ways of relating, or orientation to the extrafamilial world.

concept_definitions.name: Complementary Fit
concept_definitions.definition: A relationship where the home environment expresses relationship patterns, modes, or styles of interaction that are opposite to those pertaining in the family, often consciously selected by a family to balance or counteract a special feature of its family life.

concept_definitions.name: Non-fitting
concept_definitions.definition: A relationship where the home environment is unsuited to the family's pattern of interaction, role relationships, or values, leading to stress and dysfunction.

concept_definitions.name: Territory
concept_definitions.definition: A volume of space (such as a room or a house), the outer limits of which are defined by a boundary. A territory is identified with an individual or with a family, and is subject to his or their control.

concept_definitions.name: Boundary
concept_definitions.definition: The 'skin' of a territory; it defines the outer limit of a territory and separates one territory from another. It creates a barrier of variable impenetrability that must be overcome for communication to occur.

concept_definitions.name: Orientation
concept_definitions.definition: The direction in which a territory faces. For a house, this is the direction of the front door and majority of windows; for a room, it's the directional arrangement of seating and view from the window, providing the primary focus of attention outside the territory.

concept_definitions.name: Environmental Messages
concept_definitions.definition: Implicit communications conveyed by the physical environment, considered more potent than linguistic messages due to their non-explicit nature and difficulty in ascribing bad intent.

argument_structure: The paper first reviews existing literature on the influence of the physical home environment on family interaction, drawing from sociology, psychology, and architecture. It then introduces a conceptual framework based on 'fit' (isomorphic, complementary, non-fitting) derived from systems theory, and defines three core environmental concepts: territory, boundary, and orientation. These concepts are illustrated with brief vignettes of families in their home environments to demonstrate their impact on family functioning.
mechanism_or_causal_logic:
The physical home environment acts as a 'communication modality' that either facilitates or constrains family interaction, role relationships, values, and identities. This influence occurs through: 
1.  **Territory**: By expressing predominant modes of experience (sensory, cognitive, emotional), individual/family roles, identities (style), and communication patterns (furniture arrangement).
2.  **Boundary**: By resolving tensions between individuals/family/community, regulating accessibility (thickness, imperviousness, distance, openings), structuring transitions (rituals), and projecting the family's image.
3.  **Orientation**: By directing attention (windows, views), expressing openness to outside influence, reflecting how individuals perceive their separateness vs. family unity, and conveying feelings about neighbors/neighborhood.
When the environment 'fits' (isomorphically or complementarily) the family's needs and dynamics, it supports healthy functioning; when it 'non-fits', it creates stress and dysfunction. Environmental messages, being implicit, are particularly potent in shaping behavior and relationships.

findings.antecedent: Physical home environment
findings.consequent: Inter- and intrafamily interaction, role relationships, values, and identities
findings.mechanism: The physical environment serves as a communication modality, facilitating or constraining these aspects of family life.
findings.quote: The thesis of this paper is that the physical home environment may facilitate or constrain inter- and intrafamily interaction, role relationships, values, and identities.
findings.empirical_support_cited: Hall (33), Goffman (29), Sommer (68), Scheflen (63) on interpersonal relationships defined by space; Behrens, Meyers et al. (7) on furniture arrangement reflecting disturbed interaction; Bateson (6) on home furnished to look like a house, not to live in.

findings.antecedent: Furniture arrangement and style
findings.consequent: Interpersonal relationships and interaction in the home
findings.mechanism: Furniture arrangement defines spatial relationships, which in turn control interaction and express self-image and relationship structures.
findings.source: Physical Arrangements in the Home Environment
findings.quote: Observations by Hall (33), Goffman (29), Sommer (68), and Scheflen (63) illustrate the ways in which interpersonal relationships are defined by relationships individuals assume in space (distance, posture, seating arrangement, etc.).
findings.empirical_support_cited: Sommer (68) on seating arrangements and interaction volume; Bettelheim (10) on chair style/size/distance expressing self-image; Ruesch and Kees (61) on furniture controlling interaction.

findings.antecedent: Family members taking possession of furniture/territory
findings.consequent: Regulation of 'territory' use by other members
findings.mechanism: Possession of space leads to enforcement of rules regarding its use, defining individual or subgroup territories within the home.
findings.source: Physical Arrangements in the Home Environment
findings.quote: Phenomenological studies of families in their homes have drawn attention to the ways in which family members take possession of furniture, especially chairs, and may enforce regulation as to the use of their 'territory' by other members (Scheflen, 64).
findings.empirical_support_cited: Scheflen (64) on family members enforcing regulation of their 'territory'.

findings.antecedent: Furniture arrangement (e.g., tied down, taped shut, removed)
findings.consequent: Family's disturbed pattern of interaction
findings.mechanism: The physical environment can be a direct expression or symptom of underlying dysfunctional family dynamics, such as avoidance of confrontation.
findings.source: Physical Arrangements in the Home Environment
findings.quote: The parents, unable to respond to the child's restless behavior, avoided direct confrontation with his demands for attention; expressing this response also in their environment, most of the furniture was tied down, taped shut, or removed to the basement.
findings.empirical_support_cited: Behrens, Meyers et al. (7) case study where parents, unable to respond to child's restless behavior, avoided confrontation by tying down or removing furniture.

findings.antecedent: Shape and geometry of spaces (e.g., living room dimensions)
findings.consequent: Suitability for family's accustomed pattern of interaction
findings.mechanism: The physical dimensions and configuration of a space determine the possibilities for furniture arrangement and thus the interaction patterns it can support.
findings.source: Physical Arrangements in the Home Environment
findings.quote: A report from the Building Research Station, London (35) notes that the shape and size of the living room are important to families, since the dimensions of the living room determine whether or not furniture can be arranged in the manner felt to be suitable to the family's accustomed pattern of interaction.
findings.empirical_support_cited: Building Research Station, London (35) notes living room shape/size determines whether furniture can be arranged suitably.

findings.antecedent: Unconventional and informal geometry of spaces
findings.consequent: Acceptance of unconventional and informal style of interaction
findings.mechanism: The physical environment can implicitly signal or express values, which in turn influence the perceived appropriateness of certain interaction styles.
findings.source: Physical Arrangements in the Home Environment
findings.quote: Kaplan and McLaughlin (37) discovered that many users felt the unconventional and informal geometry of the spaces expressed an acceptance of unconventional and informal style of interaction.
findings.empirical_support_cited: Kaplan and McLaughlin (37) found users felt unconventional geometry expressed acceptance of unconventional interaction.

findings.antecedent: Geometry of the house (e.g., cellar, garret, nooks, corridors)
findings.consequent: Structural framework for memories
findings.mechanism: Distinct physical spaces within a house serve as 'refuges' for memories, making them more clearly delineated and housed.
findings.source: Physical Arrangements in the Home Environment
findings.quote: Bachelard makes the point that the geometry of the house provides a structural framework for our memories: '... thanks to the house, a great many of our memories are housed, and if the house is a bit elaborate, if it has a cellar and a garret, nooks and corridors, our memories have refuges that are all the more clearly delineated' (4, p. 8).
findings.empirical_support_cited: Bachelard (4) on geometry of house providing framework for memories.

findings.antecedent: Nonhuman environment
findings.consequent: Individual's mental development and sense of identity
findings.mechanism: The physical surroundings contribute significantly to the formation of self and identity, similar to social contact.
findings.source: Physical Arrangements in the Home Environment
findings.quote: Searles (65) has suggested that the nonhuman environment may be as significant in the individual's mental development and sense of identity as is social contact.
findings.empirical_support_cited: Searles (65) suggests nonhuman environment is as significant as social contact for mental development/identity; Cooper (14) explores house as extension of self.

findings.antecedent: Spatial relationship of rooms (dwelling plan)
findings.consequent: Family interactional implications
findings.mechanism: The layout of rooms dictates proximity, privacy, and ease of gathering, thereby influencing interaction patterns.
findings.source: Physical Arrangements in the Home Environment
findings.quote: The plan of a dwelling-that is, the spatial relationship of rooms to each other-has been noticed by many observers to carry important interactional implications for the family.
findings.empirical_support_cited: Many observers have noted the interactional implications of dwelling plans.

findings.antecedent: Inadequate provisions for privacy and communication in a house plan
findings.consequent: Conflict within and between subgroups of a family
findings.mechanism: Lack of appropriate spatial arrangements for privacy and communication prevents family members from achieving necessary personal space and ease of interaction, leading to friction.
findings.source: Physical Arrangements in the Home Environment
findings.quote: Inadequate provisions for privacy and communication lead to conflict, adequate provisions foster cooperation. The fundamental scheme of the house grows out of such considerations as these.
findings.empirical_support_cited: Kennedy (38) states that inadequate provisions lead to conflict, while adequate provisions foster cooperation.

findings.antecedent: Habitable space per person (dwelling unit)
findings.consequent: Levels of tension among family members
findings.mechanism: The amount of available space directly impacts perceived crowding and personal space, which in turn affects psychological comfort and interpersonal friction.
findings.source: Physical Arrangements in the Home Environment
findings.quote: De Lauwe (17) argues that the habitable space per person in a dwelling unit has a strong effect on the levels of tension among the members of the family.
findings.empirical_support_cited: De Lauwe (17) argues strong effect; Mitchell (49) indicates congestion relates to stress; Bernstein (9) suggests congestion affects children's language/perceptions.

findings.antecedent: Crowding in a dwelling unit
findings.consequent: Mental illness
findings.mechanism: Chronic lack of personal space and increased interpersonal friction due to crowding can contribute to psychological distress and pathology.
findings.source: Physical Arrangements in the Home Environment
findings.quote: Other researchers have argued that crowding in a dwelling unit has demonstratably contributed to mental illness (16, 42, 79).
findings.empirical_support_cited: Other researchers have argued demonstrably contributed (16, 42, 79).

findings.antecedent: Small kitchens
findings.consequent: Problems for housewives trying to cook and cope with children/adults
findings.mechanism: Limited space in a key functional area creates practical difficulties and stress when multiple activities or individuals compete for that space.
findings.source: Physical Arrangements in the Home Environment
findings.quote: Hall (32) found that small kitchens created problems for housewives trying simultaneously to cook and cope with children or other adults.
findings.empirical_support_cited: Hall (32) found small kitchens created problems; other studies (3, 58) suggest kitchen is most important room.

findings.antecedent: Territory (space claimed as one's own)
findings.consequent: Sense of individuality and autonomy
findings.mechanism: Having a defined personal space that one controls allows for self-expression and a feeling of independence.
findings.source: Physical Arrangements in the Home Environment
findings.quote: Smith's definition of territory, 'encapsulated zones of autonomy,' (66) captures the sense of individuality that may be fostered by possession of a territory.
findings.empirical_support_cited: Smith's (66) definition of territory as 'encapsulated zones of autonomy' captures this sense.

findings.antecedent: Architect's decisions in designing house/site plan
findings.consequent: Nature of group memberships imposed upon residents
findings.mechanism: Design choices pre-determine social opportunities and constraints, influencing who residents interact with and how they are perceived by outsiders.
findings.quote: The decisions of the architect in designing the house, in laying out the site plan for a group of houses, determine to a large extent the nature of the group memberships which will be imposed upon the residents of the houses.
findings.empirical_support_cited: Festinger (21) in his analysis of friendship patterns among students.

findings.antecedent: Orientation, accessibility, functional and physical distance between dwellings
findings.consequent: Friendship patterns
findings.mechanism: These spatial factors influence the likelihood and ease of encounters, which are foundational for forming social bonds.
findings.quote: Festinger found that orientation, accessibility, functional and physical distance influence friendship patterns.
findings.empirical_support_cited: Festinger (21) found these factors influence friendship patterns; Form (24) and Whyte (76) reported connection between proximity and friendship.

findings.antecedent: Close proximity of neighbors and relatives (e.g., in slums)
findings.consequent: Frequent contacts, deep involvement in family life, closeness to larger community
findings.mechanism: Physical closeness increases opportunities for spontaneous interaction and mutual support, strengthening social ties.
findings.quote: Mogey's (50) study of workers living in slums showed that the close proximity of neighbors and relatives fostered frequent contacts, a deep involvement in one another's family life, and considerable closeness to the larger community of people.
findings.empirical_support_cited: Mogey's (50) study of workers in slums; Willmott and Young (78, 80) on large/small group formation in new estates.

findings.antecedent: Proximity between dwellings
findings.consequent: Enmity as well as friendships
findings.mechanism: While proximity can foster positive social bonds, it also increases potential for conflict due to lack of privacy or increased friction.
findings.quote: Wallace (72) points out that proximity may increase enmity as well as friendships and discusses the importance of designing for privacy in a neighborhood.
findings.empirical_support_cited: Wallace (72) points out proximity may increase enmity; Cooper (15) found residents wanted more privacy from neighbors.

findings.antecedent: Location and orientation of major openings (doors, windows)
findings.consequent: Friendship formation and social interaction
findings.mechanism: Openings provide opportunities for visual and verbal contact, facilitating spontaneous social engagement and observation.
findings.quote: The location and orientation of the major openings (doors, windows) are shown by Festinger (21) to be important in friendship formation.
findings.empirical_support_cited: Festinger (21) and Kuper (41) on importance for friendship; Goffman (30) on windows for partial participation; Gans (27) and Jacobs (36) on windows facilitating social interaction.

findings.antecedent: High-rise apartment buildings (lack of easy interaction through windows, unsupervised areas)
findings.consequent: Problems in supervision of small children, mother's anxiety, children's independence, crime and vandalism
findings.mechanism: Lack of visual connection to outdoor play areas and presence of unobserved public spaces prevent natural surveillance, leading to safety concerns and restricted child autonomy.
findings.quote: Wallace (73) shows that high-rise apartments do not allow for easy interaction through the windows and hence create problems in the supervision of small children.
findings.empirical_support_cited: Wallace (73) on supervision problems; Hall (33) on unsupervised areas; Kumove (40) on children's independence; Rainwater (57) and Newman (53) on crime/vandalism.

findings.antecedent: Shared boundaries (walls, floors) in multi-family dwellings that do not allow for natural interactional links
findings.consequent: Variety of problems (e.g., noise annoyance, feeling of not being able to be noisy, mental health effects on children)
findings.mechanism: Inadequate sound and visual separation in shared living spaces leads to perceived lack of privacy, annoyance, and psychological constriction.
findings.quote: More annoying than the noise made by neighbors is the feeling that residents report of not being able to be noisy themselves (Raven, 59).
findings.empirical_support_cited: Raven (59) on noise annoyance; Willis (77) on constriction on children's noise-making.

findings.antecedent: Physical environment (e.g., public/semi-private territories, shared facilities, dwelling relationships)
findings.consequent: Social structure and interaction patterns of inhabitants
findings.mechanism: The design and arrangement of shared spaces and the relationships between buildings directly support or hinder specific social organizations and interaction styles.
findings.quote: The character of the public and semi-private territories, the function and quality of the shared facilities, and the general physical relationships between dwellings are cited by a number of researchers as significantly related to the social structure of its inhabitants and to the patterns of interaction among families.
findings.empirical_support_cited: Van Eyck (71), Levi-Strauss (43), Sim Van der Ryn (70) on architecture reflecting social organization; Petonnet (55) on use of public areas in housing project; Gans (27) on Boston's West End.

findings.antecedent: Institutional image of public housing schemes
findings.consequent: Negative self-image, sense of institutional helplessness, separation from others for low-income residents
findings.mechanism: The design and aesthetic of public housing can reinforce societal stigmas associated with poverty, impacting residents' self-perception and social integration.
findings.quote: To the majority of the poor housed in low-income, mass housing in this country, however, the institutional image of the public housing schemes in which they live has a more devastating effect, for it reinforces a negative self-image, sense of institutional helplessness, and separation from others that they may well associate with the vicious cycle of being poor (Newman, 53).
findings.empirical_support_cited: Newman (53) on devastating effect of institutional image.

findings.antecedent: Arrangement of buildings, streets, and open spaces (or lack thereof) that promotes easy availability of person to person
findings.consequent: Strong, frequent, and intensive interaction with a large number of relatives (working-class areas)
findings.mechanism: Physical layouts that maximize opportunities for casual encounters and minimize barriers to social contact support dense, interconnected social networks.
findings.quote: Michelson (47), in a review of the literature on the sociology of the urban environment states that, in all the studies of urban ghettos, a common finding is that 'an emphasis on the life style which includes very strong, frequent and intensive interaction with a large number of relatives seems to require that they live in some arrangement of buildings, streets and open spaces (or the lack of them) that promotes the easy availability of person to person.'
findings.empirical_support_cited: Fried and Gleicher (25) on working-class areas; Michelson (47) on urban ghettos; Jacobs (36) on Greenwich Village; Marris (45) on Lagos slums.

findings.antecedent: Move to suburbs (from slums/multi-family compounds)
findings.consequent: Destruction of extended family interaction patterns, shift to nuclear family emphasis, focus on possessions, role changes (e.g., women from traders to housewives)
findings.mechanism: Suburban housing designs (e.g., row houses for nuclear families) and associated environments (e.g., lack of communal spaces, distance from work) physically disrupt traditional social structures and enforce new roles and values.
findings.quote: The studies of life style in suburban settings show a very different pattern of interfamily relationships from those prevalent in the ghettos. The studies of families who moved from the slums to the suburbs (Willmott and Young, 78, 80; Mogey, 51) show that in each case their extended family interaction patterns were destroyed.
findings.empirical_support_cited: Marris (45) on Lagos; Marris and Berger (8) on role changes; Willmott and Young (78, 80) and Mogey (51) on destruction of extended family patterns.

findings.antecedent: High-rise apartments
findings.consequent: Anonymity and isolation
findings.mechanism: The design of high-rise complexes often limits opportunities for casual social interaction and creates a sense of detachment from neighbors.
findings.quote: Most early studies of high-rise apartments focused on physical and mental morbidity; Michelson (48) and Zito (81) both found a high degree of anonymity and isolation within the high rise complexes studied.
findings.empirical_support_cited: Michelson (48) and Zito (81) found high degree of anonymity and isolation.

findings.antecedent: Home environment isomorphically fitting family's identity, way of relating, or orientation
findings.consequent: Support for family's social life and dynamics
findings.mechanism: When the physical environment mirrors or expresses the family's internal characteristics, it reinforces and supports those characteristics, leading to a sense of coherence and ease.
findings.quote: The family's strong sense of its unique family identity is expressed isomorphically by the powerful geometry of its free-standing house and the physical separation of its house from others by the high-walled and tree-lined garden.
findings.empirical_support_cited: Vignette A: Family A's isolated house and garden isomorphic with their few social contacts and unique identity; open plan house isomorphic with interdependent family lacking individual identity; ultra-modern house isomorphic with rational family interaction; father's loft study isomorphic with his role and accessibility.

findings.antecedent: Home environment complementarily fitting family's style of interaction
findings.consequent: Balance and enhancement of family's way of life, development of separate identities, self-reliance
findings.mechanism: When the physical environment provides a contrasting or balancing element to the family's inherent dynamics, it can help foster desired qualities or mitigate potential excesses (e.g., separate rooms for a very close family to encourage individuality).
findings.quote: Family 'B' made the decision a few years ago to move into a house that would help to balance and enhance their way of life by providing a complementary fit for their style of interaction.
findings.empirical_support_cited: Vignette B: Close, strong-identity family chose house with minimal family areas and separate private rooms to aid development of separate identities; emotional family chose modern, functional, bland house as non-emotional background.

findings.antecedent: Home environment non-fitting family's style of interaction and needs
findings.consequent: Visible stress, anxiety, danger, overly noisy/demanding children
findings.mechanism: When the physical environment is unsuited to the family's needs, it creates practical difficulties, hinders desired interactions, and generates psychological discomfort and behavioral problems.
findings.quote: Family 'C' illustrates the ways in which an environment may be non-fitting to the style of interaction and needs of the family.
findings.empirical_support_cited: Vignette C: House designed for older children non-fitting for small boys (isolated kitchen, dangerous stairs, open living room unsuitable for play) leading to mother's anxiety and children's behavior problems.

findings.antecedent: Territory (volume of space identified with individual/family)
findings.consequent: Expression of predominant mode of 'experiencing' the world (sensations, cognitive functions, emotions)
findings.mechanism: The design, materials, and organization of a territory can be chosen or evolve to reflect and reinforce the primary sensory, intellectual, or emotional orientation of its inhabitants.
findings.quote: A territory can express the individual's or family's predominant mode of 'experiencing' the world. If sensations are predominant, the territory may accentuate sculptural, visual, tactile qualities.

findings.antecedent: Territory (volume of space identified with individual/family)
findings.consequent: Expression of individual's/family's role and identity
findings.mechanism: The functional aspects (equipment) and style of a territory communicate the primary patterns of behavior and the overall sense of self or group identity.
findings.quote: Territories can express an individual's role in a family or the role the family feels it has in society. Equipment, or the functional aspect of the furniture and objects, will express the primary patterns of behavior of the individual or the family and, hence, will express their role.

findings.antecedent: Arrangement of furniture in a territory
findings.consequent: Communication patterns (who interacts with whom, how much, manner)
findings.mechanism: Furniture arrangement dictates proximity, visual access, and conversational groupings, thereby directly influencing the flow and nature of communication.
findings.quote: Communication patterns — who interacts with whom, how much, whether in a manner that reinforces or obstructs relationships, etc. — may be expressed by the arrangement of furniture in the territory.

findings.antecedent: Boundary (e.g., wall, fabric, imaginary line)
findings.consequent: Resolution of specific tension (individual/family, family/community, community/individual)
findings.mechanism: Boundaries are physical or social constructs that define separation and connection, thereby managing the inherent conflicts between different levels of social organization.
findings.quote: Every boundary may also be viewed as a resolution of a specific tension that exists between individual and family, between family and community, between community and individual.

findings.antecedent: Thickness, imperviousness, distance from family spaces of a boundary
findings.consequent: Degree to which individual feels inaccessible to family (or family to neighborhood)
findings.mechanism: Physical characteristics of a boundary directly determine the ease or difficulty of crossing it, thus influencing perceived social distance and privacy.
findings.quote: The degree to which the individual feels inaccessible to the family (or family to the neighborhood) may be expressed in the thickness of the boundary, its degree of imperviousness, the distance from family spaces.

findings.antecedent: Boundary broken by doors, windows, proximity to family spaces
findings.consequent: Degree to which individual feels accessible to family (or family to individual)
findings.mechanism: Openings and close proximity reduce physical and psychological barriers, increasing opportunities for interaction and perceived availability.
findings.quote: The degree to which the individual feels accessible to the family (or family to the individual) may be expressed in these physical boundaries by the degree to which the boundary is broken by doors, windows, its proximity to family spaces, etc.

findings.antecedent: Threshold (main entrance to house)
findings.consequent: Passage between two different worlds of experience (self/others, alien/friend)
findings.mechanism: The threshold acts as a symbolic and physical point of transition, marking the shift from one social context or state of being to another.
findings.quote: The threshold, the main entrance to the house, is the place at which passage between two different worlds (of experience of self and relation to others - alien to member, stranger to friend) - becomes possible.

findings.antecedent: Degree of ritual necessary to cross a threshold
findings.consequent: Degree of difference experienced by the family between inside and outside
findings.mechanism: More significant perceived differences between internal and external social worlds necessitate more elaborate rituals to manage the transition and psychological adjustment.
findings.quote: The degree of ritual necessary may express the degree of difference experienced by the family between inside and outside.

findings.antecedent: Orientation of a house (direction of front door, majority of windows)
findings.consequent: Expression of degree to which one looks outside for stimulation and is open to outside influence
findings.mechanism: The primary direction a house faces, and the placement/size of its openings, physically directs attention and visual access, thereby influencing engagement with the external world.
findings.quote: Orientation can express the degree to which one looks outside oneself for stimulation and the degree to which one is open to influence from outside the immediate family system.

findings.antecedent: Many large windows in a house
findings.consequent: Attention frequently oriented toward events/objects outside the house
findings.mechanism: Large windows provide extensive visual access to the external environment, naturally drawing attention outwards.
findings.quote: If there are a great many large windows, one's attention may frequently be oriented toward events or objects outside the boundary of the house.

findings.antecedent: Few and tiny windows in a house
findings.consequent: Attention restricted to what is happening within the house
findings.mechanism: Limited visual access to the outside world reduces external distractions, focusing attention inwards.
findings.quote: Very few and tiny windows would tend to restrict one's attention to what is happening within the house.

findings.antecedent: Distance of the view from the window
findings.consequent: Expression of how far outside the family situation one looks for stimulation and what kind of stimulation is perceived
findings.mechanism: The scope and content of the view (e.g., busy streets vs. wide valleys) symbolically and practically influences the type of external engagement and thought processes it encourages.
findings.quote: The distance of the view from the window can be expressive of how far outside the family situation one looks for stimulation and what kind of stimulation is perceived to lie outside the family.

findings.antecedent: Comparative orientation of family spaces and individual spaces to sun and view
findings.consequent: Expression of how individuals feel their experience of being separate is different from their experience of being a family
findings.mechanism: Differential access to desirable environmental qualities (sun, views) in shared vs. private spaces can symbolize and reinforce perceived levels of individual autonomy versus family integration.
findings.quote: The comparative orientation of family spaces and individual spaces to sun and view may be expressive of how the individuals feel their experience of being separate is different from their experience of being a family.

findings.antecedent: Orientation of the front door (toward or away from the street) and relationship between house and neighborhood
findings.consequent: Feelings that the family has about its orientation toward its neighbors and neighborhood
findings.mechanism: The design of the entrance and the house's relationship to its surroundings physically manifest the family's desired level of engagement or detachment from the community.
findings.quote: The feelings that the family has about its orientation toward its neighbors and its neighborhood may be expressed by the orientation of the front door (toward or away from the street) and in the relationship between the house itself and its neighborhood (attractive or exciting places nearby).

findings.antecedent: Incongruence between parental verbal messages and home environmental messages (e.g., unequal room assignment with claims of equal devotion)
findings.consequent: Difficulties for family members to articulate, question, or oppose environmental messages
findings.mechanism: Environmental messages are implicit and non-explicit, making them more potent and harder to challenge than verbal messages, similar to how paralinguistic messages take precedence over linguistic ones.
findings.quote: Environmental messages may be more potent in their impact, just as paralinguistic messages are considered to take precedence over linguistic ones in that they are not made explicit and bad intent cannot be easily ascribed. They thus become more difficult to articulate, question, or oppose.

testable_hypotheses_or_predictions: Families living in environments that are 'isomorphically fitting' to their social patterns will report higher environmental satisfaction and lower perceived stress compared to families in 'non-fitting' environments.

Families intentionally selecting or modifying their home environment to achieve a 'complementary fit' will demonstrate improved self-reliance and individual identity development among members, particularly in areas where the environment counteracts existing family dynamics.

The degree of 'non-fit' between a family's needs (e.g., for child supervision, quiet spaces) and the physical home environment (e.g., isolated kitchens, dangerous stairs, open-plan living rooms) will correlate with increased parental anxiety and observed behavioral problems in children.

The 'thickness' or 'imperviousness' of boundaries within a home will predict the perceived inaccessibility of individual family members to others, influencing privacy regulation and interaction frequency.
The orientation of a house's windows and front door will predict the family's reported engagement with and feelings towards their neighborhood and the external world.

Environmental messages that are incongruent with explicit verbal messages (e.g., claiming equal treatment while providing unequal spaces) will lead to greater psychological distress and difficulty in challenging perceived inequities among family members.
bridge_warrants: The paper explicitly draws on systems theory for the concepts of 'isomorphism' and 'complementarity' to describe man-environment relationships.
It connects the physical environment to communication theory by positing the environment as a 'communication modality' alongside linguistic and paralinguistic forms.

The framework integrates concepts from sociology (e.g., social organization, group membership), psychology (e.g., self-image, identity, mental development), and child development (e.g., age-specific needs) into an architectural context.
Kurt Lewin's field theory concepts of 'life space' and 'barriers' are explicitly linked to their physical environmental equivalents, bridging social psychology with architectural space.
methodological_critiques: Systematic attention to the physical aspects of family environments is much overdue.
Existing research on family interaction and the home environment has largely failed to take a specifically interactionist approach, focusing instead on functional housekeeping issues.
Few researchers have turned their attention to the specific ways in which families alter features of their physical environment to support accustomed interactional patterns.

The study of environments requires the development of a methodology that includes the inspection of the family's physical surroundings (photographs and drawings of plans), observations of the family's behavior within its environment, and interviews with the family as a whole and with individual members, focused on their use and reaction to their environment and conducted by investigators with clinical skills.
model_structure: The proposed conceptual framework posits that the 'fit' between a family's internal dynamics (interaction, roles, values, identities) and its physical home environment (described by territory, boundary, and orientation) determines the quality of family functioning. This 'fit' can be isomorphic (similar patterns), complementary (balancing opposites), or non-fitting (unsuited). The environment acts as a potent, often implicit, communication modality that can either facilitate or constrain family life.
limitations: The paper's hypotheses are subject to confirmation or modification on the basis of studies whose results and methodology will be described in subsequent papers, implying that the current paper is primarily theoretical and illustrative.
